Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Local-anesthetic injection pain

PBM may reduce pain from local-anesthetic needle puncture in selected dental procedures, but trial results vary by age, injection site, and pain measure. The newest synthesis found favorable average effects on several scales while rating certainty very low.

Summary of the Evidence

PBM may reduce pain during local-anesthetic needle puncture in some dental procedures, but the size and reliability of the effect remain uncertain. The newest synthesis found lower pain scores on three of four pooled scales, while a previous review found mostly null results. Results differ by injection site, age, topical-anesthetic use, and pain measure.

Human and clinical evidence

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis included 27 randomized trials with 1,519 participants, with 25 trials contributing to pooled estimates. PBM reduced pain scores on the visual analogue scale, pain-rating scale, and FLACC behavioral scale, but not on the Sound-Eye-Motor scale. The review rated certainty very low for all outcomes because estimates varied widely, prediction intervals were broad, and studies had methodological concerns (da Silva Nascimento et al. 2026).

A small three-group randomized trial in 15 children illustrates that results depend on the pain measure: Buzzy produced the most favorable behavioral ratings, while PBM had lower self-reported pain than topical gel (Shrutha et al. 2024). A 2025 review of 14 studies found mixed results in children: three studies favored PBM on the Wong-Baker scale but not on FLACC, while three reported no significant difference from topical anesthesia. Among adults, five studies reported lower pain, although one statistically significant difference was judged too small to be clinically meaningful (Shekarchi et al. 2025). A 2024 review of eight trials found no significant pain difference in most included studies, and none was judged at low risk of bias (Mesquita et al. 2024).

In a randomized trial of 64 children aged five to seven, 660-nm PBM before infiltration injection reduced heart-rate and behavioral pain indicators compared with topical anesthetic gel. It did not change pain indicators during the later pulpotomy or stainless-steel crown procedure, so the finding concerns injection discomfort rather than anesthetic success (Hamouda et al. 2024). By contrast, a triple-blind trial of 160 children found no injection-pain difference when 940-nm PBM was delivered for 20, 30, or 40 seconds versus placebo (Elbay et al. 2023). A 2025 split-mouth trial reported lower pain during inferior alveolar nerve block after 940-nm PBM in children aged 8–12, adding a favorable result for a specific injection site and age group (Farah et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in the exact dental injection-pain category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Trials generally apply PBM shortly before injection, often at the intended injection site, although some use laser acupuncture away from the mouth. Tested wavelengths include red and near-infrared diode lasers, with protocols spanning roughly 660–980 nm, different powers and exposure times, and doses that are incompletely reported in several records. Injection methods include buccal or palatal infiltration and inferior alveolar nerve block. Some trials compare PBM with sham, while others use topical anesthetic or combine the two. No optimal regimen has been established.

Interpretation

Current evidence supports a possible short-term reduction in injection pain, especially in selected pediatric settings, but confidence is very low. Several trials report null results, and statistically significant differences do not always translate into clinically important reductions. Studies should standardize injection techniques and pain scales, mask assessors, compare PBM with sham and usual topical care, and report anesthetic success separately from pain during needle puncture.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Visual analogue scale — VAS mean difference −1.72 (95% CI −2.87 to −0.57).

Pain-rating scale — MD −0.89 (95% CI −1.59 to −0.20). FLACC behavioral scale — MD −1.14 (95% CI −1.90 to −0.37).

Sound-Eye-Motor scale — no significant pooled difference, MD −0.56 (95% CI −1.72 to +0.60). Heterogeneity was very high across outcomes (I² = 96.7%–98.9%); certainty was very low (da Silva Nascimento et al. 2026).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for short-term reduction in pain during local-anesthetic needle puncture across dental procedures.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The 2026 review pooled 25 randomized trials and rated all pain outcomes very low certainty. Estimates differed across pain scales, with very high heterogeneity and broad prediction intervals. Earlier reviews and individual trials reached mixed conclusions, and injection site, age, topical anesthetic, and treatment parameters varied. These limits make the average effect uncertain despite favorable pooled results on several scales.
